L.8e6: ^℟.^ The Lord is risen indeed, alleluia.
L.8g0: ^℣.^ And hath appeared to Simon, alleluia.
L.dab: ^Ant.^ Allelúia, Surréxit Dóminus vere: * Veníte, adorémus, allelúia.
L.dah: ^Ant.^ Allelúja, Surréxit Dóminus vere: * Veníte, adorémus, allelúja.
L.7ho: ^34:1^ Iúdica, Dómine, nocéntes me, * expúgna impugnántes me.
L.7ia: ^34:2^ Apprehénde arma et scutum: * et exsúrge in adiutórium mihi.
L.7id: ^34:3^ Effúnde frámeam, et conclúde advérsus eos, qui persequúntur me: * dic ánimæ meæ: Salus tua ego sum.
L.7if: ^34:4^ Confundántur et revereántur, * quæréntes ánimam meam.
L.7ie: ^34:4^ Avertántur retrórsum, et confundántur * cogitántes mihi mala.
L.7ii: ^34:5^ Fiant tamquam pulvis ante fáciem venti: * et Ángelus Dómini coárctans eos.
L.7ik: ^34:6^ Fiat via illórum ténebræ et lúbricum: * et Ángelus Dómini pérsequens eos.
L.7in: ^34:7^ Quóniam gratis abscondérunt mihi intéritum láquei sui: * supervácue exprobravérunt ánimam meam.
L.7ip: ^34:8^ Véniat illi láqueus, quem ignórat: et cáptio, quam abscóndit, apprehéndat eum: * et in láqueum cadat in ipsum.
L.7ir: ^34:9^ Ánima autem mea exsultábit in Dómino: * et delectábitur super salutári suo.
L.7h3: ^34:10^ Ómnia ossa mea dicent: * Dómine, quis símilis tibi?
L.7h1: ^34:10^ Erípiens ínopem de manu fortiórum eius: * egénum et páuperem a diripiéntibus eum.
L.7hp: ^34:1^ Judge thou, O Lord, them that wrong me: * overthrow them that fight against me.
L.7ib: ^34:2^ Take hold of arms and shield: * and rise up to help me.
L.7ic: ^34:3^ Bring out the sword, and shut up the way against them that persecute me: * say to my soul: I am thy salvation.
L.7ig: ^34:4^ Let them be confounded and ashamed * that seek after my soul.
L.7ih: ^34:4^ Let them be turned back and be confounded * that devise against me.
L.7ij: ^34:5^ Let them become as dust before the wind: * and let the Angel of the Lord straiten them.
L.7il: ^34:6^ Let their way become dark and slippery; * and let the Angel of the Lord pursue them.
L.7im: ^34:7^ For without cause they have hidden their net for me unto destruction: * without cause they have upbraided my soul.
L.7io: ^34:8^ Let the snare which he knoweth not come upon him: and let the net which he hath hidden catch him: * and into that very snare let them fall.
L.7iq: ^34:9^ But my soul shall rejoice in the Lord; * and shall be delighted in his salvation.
L.7h0: ^34:10^ All my bones shall say: * Lord, who is like to thee?
L.7h2: ^34:10^ Who deliverest the poor from the hand of them that are stronger than he; * the needy and the poor from them that strip him.
L.7h4: ^34:11^ Surgéntes testes iníqui, * quæ ignorábam interrogábant me.
L.7h6: ^34:12^ Retribuébant mihi mala pro bonis: * sterilitátem ánimæ meæ.
L.7h9: ^34:13^ Ego autem cum mihi molésti essent, * induébar cilício.
L.7ha: ^34:13^ Humiliábam in ieiúnio ánimam meam: * et orátio mea in sinu meo convertétur.
L.7hd: ^34:14^ Quasi próximum, et quasi fratrem nostrum, sic complacébam: * quasi lugens et contristátus, sic humiliábar.
L.7hf: ^34:15^ Et advérsum me lætáti sunt, et convenérunt: * congregáta sunt super me flagélla, et ignorávi.
L.7hg: ^34:16^ Dissipáti sunt, nec compúncti, tentavérunt me, subsannavérunt me subsannatióne: * frenduérunt super me déntibus suis.
L.7hi: ^34:17^ Dómine, quando respícies? * restítue ánimam meam a malignitáte eórum, a leónibus únicam meam.
L.7h5: ^34:11^ Unjust witnesses rising up * have asked me things I knew not.
L.7h7: ^34:12^ They repaid me evil for good: * to the depriving me of my soul.
L.7h8: ^34:13^ But as for me, when they were troublesome to me, * I was clothed with haircloth.
L.7hb: ^34:13^ I humbled my soul with fasting; * and my prayer shall be turned into my bosom.
L.7hc: ^34:14^ As a neighbour and as an own brother, so did I please: * as one mourning and sorrowful so was I humbled.
L.7he: ^34:15^ But they rejoiced against me, and came together: * scourges were gathered together upon me, and I knew not.
L.7hh: ^34:16^ They were separated, and repented not: they tempted me, they scoffed at me with scorn: * they gnashed upon me with their teeth.
L.7hj: ^34:17^ Lord, when wilt thou look upon me? * rescue thou my soul from their malice: my only one from the lions.
L.7hk: ^34:18^ Confitébor tibi in ecclésia magna, * in pópulo gravi laudábo te.
L.7hn: ^34:19^ Non supergáudeant mihi qui adversántur mihi iníque: * qui odérunt me gratis et ánnuunt óculis.
L.7hr: ^34:20^ Quóniam mihi quidem pacífice loquebántur: * et in iracúndia terræ loquéntes, dolos cogitábant.
L.7ht: ^34:21^ Et dilatavérunt super me os suum: * dixérunt: Euge, euge, vidérunt óculi nostri.
L.7hv: ^34:22^ Vidísti, Dómine, ne síleas: * Dómine, ne discédas a me.
L.7hx: ^34:23^ Exsúrge et inténde iudício meo: * Deus meus, et Dóminus meus in causam meam.
L.7hy: ^34:24^ Iúdica me secúndum iustítiam tuam, Dómine, Deus meus, * et non supergáudeant mihi.
L.7i1: ^34:25^ Non dicant in córdibus suis: Euge, euge, ánimæ nostræ: * nec dicant: Devorávimus eum.
L.7i2: ^34:26^ Erubéscant et revereántur simul, * qui gratulántur malis meis.
L.7i3: ^34:26^ Induántur confusióne et reveréntia * qui magna loquúntur super me.
L.7i6: ^34:27^ Exsúltent et læténtur qui volunt iustítiam meam: * et dicant semper: Magnificétur Dóminus qui volunt pacem servi eius.
L.7i9: ^34:28^ Et lingua mea meditábitur iustítiam tuam, * tota die laudem tuam.
L.7hl: ^34:18^ I will give thanks to thee in a great church; * I will praise thee in a strong people.
L.7hm: ^34:19^ Let not them that are my enemies wrongfully rejoice over me: * who have hated me without cause, and wink with the eyes.
L.7hq: ^34:20^ For they spoke indeed peaceably to me; * and speaking in the anger of the earth they devised guile.
L.7hs: ^34:21^ And they opened their mouth wide against me; * they said: Well done, well done, our eyes have seen it.
L.7hu: ^34:22^ Thou hast seen, O Lord, be not thou silent: * O Lord, depart not from me.
L.7hw: ^34:23^ Arise, and be attentive to my judgment: * to my cause, my God, and my Lord.
L.7hz: ^34:24^ Judge me, O Lord my God according to thy justice, * and let them not rejoice over me.
L.7i0: ^34:25^ Let them not say in their hearts: It is well, it is well, to our mind: * neither let them say: We have swallowed him up.
L.7i5: ^34:26^ Let them blush: and be ashamed together, * who rejoice at my evils.
L.7i4: ^34:26^ Let them be clothed with confusion and shame, * who speak great things against me.
L.7i7: ^34:27^ Let them rejoice and be glad, who are well pleased with my justice, * and let them say always: The Lord be magnified, who delights in the peace of his servant.
L.7i8: ^34:28^ And my tongue shall meditate thy justice, * thy praise all the day long.
L.gdg: ^℟.^ The Lord is risen from the sepulchre, alleluia.
L.h8w: ^℣.^ Who for us was hanged on the tree, alleluia.
L.7q0: ^61:2^ Nonne Deo subiécta erit ánima mea? * ab ipso enim salutáre meum.
L.7q3: ^61:3^ Nam et ipse Deus meus, et salutáris meus: * suscéptor meus, non movébor ámplius.
L.7q5: ^61:4^ Quoúsque irrúitis in hóminem? * interfícitis univérsi vos: tamquam paríeti inclináto et macériæ depúlsæ?
L.7q7: ^61:5^ Verúmtamen prétium meum cogitavérunt repéllere, cucúrri in siti: * ore suo benedicébant, et corde suo maledicébant.
L.7q9: ^61:6^ Verúmtamen Deo subiécta esto, ánima mea: * quóniam ab ipso patiéntia mea.
L.7qb: ^61:7^ Quia ipse Deus meus, et salvátor meus: * adiútor meus, non emigrábo.
L.7qc: ^61:8^ In Deo salutáre meum, et glória mea: * Deus auxílii mei, et spes mea in Deo est.
L.7qe: ^61:9^ Speráte in eo omnis congregátio pópuli, effúndite coram illo corda vestra: * Deus adiútor noster in ætérnum.
L.7pv: ^61:10^ Verúmtamen vani fílii hóminum, mendáces fílii hóminum in statéris: * ut decípiant ipsi de vanitáte in idípsum.
L.7pw: ^61:11^ Nolíte speráre in iniquitáte, et rapínas nolíte concupíscere: * divítiæ si áffluant, nolíte cor appónere.
L.7pz: ^61:12^ Semel locútus est Deus, duo hæc audívi, quia potéstas Dei est, et tibi, Dómine, misericórdia: * quia tu reddes unicuíque iuxta ópera sua.
L.7q1: ^61:2^ Shall not my soul be subject to God? * for from him is my salvation.
L.7q2: ^61:3^ For he is my God and my saviour: * he is my protector, I shall be moved no more.
L.7q4: ^61:4^ How long do you rush in upon a man? * you all kill, as if you were thrusting down a leaning wall, and a tottering fence.
L.7q6: ^61:5^ But they have thought to cast away my price; I ran in thirst: * they blessed with their mouth, but cursed with their heart.
L.7q8: ^61:6^ But be thou, O my soul, subject to God: * for from him is my patience.
L.7qa: ^61:7^ For he is my God and my saviour: * he is my helper, I shall not be moved.
L.7qd: ^61:8^ In God is my salvation and my glory: * he is the God of my help, and my hope is in God.
L.7qf: ^61:9^ Trust in him, all ye congregation of people: pour out your hearts before him. * God is our helper for ever.
L.7pu: ^61:10^ But vain are the sons of men, the sons of men are liars in the balances: * that by vanity they may together deceive.
L.7px: ^61:11^ Trust not in iniquity, and cover not robberies: * if riches abound, set not your heart upon them.
L.7py: ^61:12^ God hath spoken once, these two things have I heard, that power belongeth to God, and mercy to thee, O Lord; * for thou wilt render to every man according to his works.
L.7sv: ^77:1^ Atténdite, pópule meus, legem meam: * inclináte aurem vestram in verba oris mei.
L.7ti: ^77:2^ Apériam in parábolis os meum: * loquar propositiónes ab inítio.
L.7u7: ^77:3^ Quanta audívimus et cognóvimus ea: * et patres nostri narravérunt nobis.
L.7uu: ^77:4^ Non sunt occultáta a fíliis eórum: * in generatióne áltera.
L.7ut: ^77:4^ Narrántes laudes Dómini, et virtútes eius: * et mirabília eius, quæ fecit.
L.7vj: ^77:5^ Et suscitávit testimónium in Iacob: * et legem pósuit in Israël.
L.7vl: ^77:5^ Quanta mandávit pátribus nostris nota fácere ea fíliis suis: * ut cognóscat generátio áltera.
L.7w6: ^77:6^ Fílii qui nascéntur, et exsúrgent, * et narrábunt fíliis suis.
L.7wf: ^77:7^ Ut ponant in Deo spem suam, et non obliviscántur óperum Dei: * et mandáta eius exquírant.
L.7wi: ^77:8^ Ne fiant sicut patres eórum: * generátio prava et exásperans.
L.7wh: ^77:8^ Generátio, quæ non diréxit cor suum: * et non est créditus cum Deo spíritus eius.
L.7su: ^77:1^ Attend, O my people, to my law: * incline your ears to the words of my mouth.
L.7tj: ^77:2^ I will open my mouth in parables: * I will utter propositions from the beginning.
L.7u6: ^77:3^ How great things have we heard and known, * and our fathers have told us.
L.7uv: ^77:4^ They have not been hidden from their children, * in another generation.
L.7us: ^77:4^ Declaring the praises of the Lord, and his powers, * and his wonders which he hath done.
L.7vi: ^77:5^ And he set up a testimony in Jacob: * and made a law in Israel.
L.7vk: ^77:5^ How great things he commanded our fathers, that they should make the same known to their children: * that another generation might know them.
L.7w7: ^77:6^ The children that should be born and should rise up, * and declare them to their children.
L.7we: ^77:7^ That they may put their hope in God and may not forget the works of God: * and may seek his commandments.
L.7wj: ^77:8^ That they may not become like their fathers, * a perverse and exasperating generation.
L.7wg: ^77:8^ A generation that set not their heart aright: * and whose spirit was not faithful to God.
L.7wk: ^77:9^ Fílii Ephrem intendéntes et mitténtes arcum: * convérsi sunt in die belli.
L.7sa: ^77:10^ Non custodiérunt testaméntum Dei: * et in lege eius noluérunt ambuláre.
L.7sd: ^77:11^ Et oblíti sunt benefactórum eius: * et mirabílium eius quæ osténdit eis.
L.7se: ^77:12^ Coram pátribus eórum fecit mirabília in terra Ægýpti: * in campo Táneos.
L.7sh: ^77:13^ Interrúpit mare, et perdúxit eos: * et státuit aquas quasi in utre.
L.7sj: ^77:14^ Et dedúxit eos in nube diéi: * et tota nocte in illuminatióne ignis.
L.7sl: ^77:15^ Interrúpit petram in erémo: * et adaquávit eos velut in abýsso multa.
L.7sm: ^77:16^ Et edúxit aquam de petra: * et dedúxit tamquam flúmina aquas.
L.7wl: ^77:9^ The sons of Ephraim who bend and shoot with the bow: * they have turned back in the day of battle.
L.7sb: ^77:10^ They kept not the covenant of God: * and in his law they would not walk.
L.7sc: ^77:11^ And they forgot his benefits, * and his wonders that he had shewn them.
L.7sf: ^77:12^ Wonderful things did he do in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, * in the field of Tanis.
L.7sg: ^77:13^ He divided the sea and brought them through: * and he made the waters to stand as in a vessel.
L.7si: ^77:14^ And he conducted them with a cloud by day: * and all the night with a light of fire.
L.7sk: ^77:15^ He struck the rock in the wilderness: * and gave them to drink, as out of the great deep.
L.7sn: ^77:16^ He brought forth water out of the rock: * and made streams run down as rivers.
L.7sp: ^77:17^ Et apposuérunt adhuc peccáre ei: * in iram excitavérunt Excélsum in inaquóso.
L.7sr: ^77:18^ Et tentavérunt Deum in córdibus suis, * ut péterent escas animábus suis.
L.7st: ^77:19^ Et male locúti sunt de Deo: * dixérunt: Numquid póterit Deus paráre mensam in desérto?
L.7sz: ^77:20^ Quóniam percússit petram, et fluxérunt aquæ: * et torréntes inundavérunt.
L.7sy: ^77:20^ Numquid et panem póterit dare, * aut paráre mensam pópulo suo?
L.7t1: ^77:21^ Ídeo audívit Dóminus, et dístulit: * et ignis accénsus est in Iacob, et ira ascéndit in Israël.
L.7t3: ^77:22^ Quia non credidérunt in Deo: * nec speravérunt in salutári eius:
L.7t5: ^77:23^ Et mandávit núbibus désuper: * et iánuas cæli apéruit.
L.7t7: ^77:24^ Et pluit illis manna ad manducándum: * et panem cæli dedit eis.
L.7t9: ^77:25^ Panem Angelórum manducávit homo, * cibária misit eis in abundántia.
L.7tb: ^77:26^ Tránstulit Austrum de cælo: * et indúxit in virtúte sua Áfricum.
L.7td: ^77:27^ Et pluit super eos sicut púlverem carnes: * et sicut arénam maris volatília pennáta.
L.7tf: ^77:28^ Et cecidérunt in médio castrórum eórum: * circa tabernácula eórum.
L.7tg: ^77:29^ Et manducavérunt, et saturáti sunt nimis, et desidérium eórum áttulit eis: * non sunt fraudáti a desidério suo.
L.7tk: ^77:30^ Adhuc escæ eórum erant in ore ipsórum: * et ira Dei ascéndit super eos.
L.7tn: ^77:31^ Et occídit pingues eórum, * et eléctos Israël impedívit.
L.7so: ^77:17^ And they added yet more sin against him: * they provoked the most High to wrath in the place without water.
L.7sq: ^77:18^ And they tempted God in their hearts, * by asking meat for their desires.
L.7ss: ^77:19^ And they spoke ill of God: * they said: Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?
L.7sw: ^77:20^ Because he struck the rock, and the waters gushed out, * and the streams overflowed.
L.7sx: ^77:20^ Can he also give bread, * or provide a table for his people?
L.7t0: ^77:21^ Therefore the Lord heard, and was angry: * and a fire was kindled against Jacob, and wrath came up against Israel.
L.7t2: ^77:22^ Because they believed not in God: * and trusted not in his salvation.
L.7t4: ^77:23^ And he had commanded the clouds from above, * and had opened the doors of heaven.
L.7t6: ^77:24^ And had rained down manna upon them to eat, * and had given them the bread of heaven.
L.7t8: ^77:25^ Man ate the bread of angels: * he sent them provisions in abundance.
L.7ta: ^77:26^ He removed the south wind from heaven: * and by his power brought in the southwest wind.
L.7tc: ^77:27^ And he rained upon them flesh as dust: * and feathered fowls like as the sand of the sea.
L.7te: ^77:28^ And they fell in the midst of their camp, * round about their pavilions.
L.7th: ^77:29^ So they did eat, and were filled exceedingly, and he gave them their desire: * they were not defrauded of that which they craved.
L.7tl: ^77:30^ As yet their meat was in their mouth: * and the wrath of God came upon them.
L.7tm: ^77:31^ And he slew the fat ones amongst them, * and brought down the chosen men of Israel.
L.6y8: ^104:1^ Confitémini Dómino, et invocáte nomen eius: * annuntiáte inter gentes ópera eius.
L.6ys: ^104:2^ Cantáte ei, et psállite ei: * narráte ómnia mirabília eius.
L.6zf: ^104:3^ Laudámini in nómine sancto eius: * lætétur cor quæréntium Dóminum.
L.6zs: ^104:4^ Quǽrite Dóminum, et confirmámini: * quǽrite fáciem eius semper.
L.6zu: ^104:5^ Mementóte mirabílium eius, quæ fecit: * prodígia eius, et iudícia oris eius.
L.6zx: ^104:6^ Semen Ábraham, servi eius: * fílii Iacob, elécti eius.
L.6zz: ^104:7^ Ipse Dóminus Deus noster: * in univérsa terra iudícia eius.
L.701: ^104:8^ Memor fuit in sǽculum testaménti sui: * verbi, quod mandávit in mille generatiónes:
L.702: ^104:9^ Quod dispósuit ad Ábraham: * et iuraménti sui ad Isaac:
L.6xp: ^104:10^ Et státuit illud Iacob in præcéptum: * et Israël in testaméntum ætérnum:
L.6xq: ^104:11^ Dicens: Tibi dabo terram Chánaan, * funículum hereditátis vestræ.
L.6xs: ^104:12^ Cum essent número brevi, * paucíssimi et íncolæ eius:
L.6xv: ^104:13^ Et pertransiérunt de gente in gentem, * et de regno ad pópulum álterum.
L.6xx: ^104:14^ Non relíquit hóminem nocére eis: * et corrípuit pro eis reges.
L.6xy: ^104:15^ Nolíte tángere christos meos: * et in prophétis meis nolíte malignári.
L.6y9: ^104:1^ Give glory to the Lord, and call upon his name: * declare his deeds among the Gentiles.
L.6yt: ^104:2^ Sing to him, yea sing praises to him: * relate all his wondrous works.
L.6ze: ^104:3^ Glory ye in his holy name: * let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord.
L.6zt: ^104:4^ Seek ye the Lord, and be strengthened: * seek his face evermore.
L.6zv: ^104:5^ Remember his marvellous works which he hath done; * his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth.
L.6zw: ^104:6^ O ye seed of Abraham his servant; * ye sons of Jacob his chosen.
L.6zy: ^104:7^ He is the Lord our God: * his judgments are in all the earth.
L.700: ^104:8^ He hath remembered his covenant for ever: * the word which he commanded to a thousand generations.
L.703: ^104:9^ Which he made to Abraham; * and his oath to Isaac:
L.6xo: ^104:10^ And he appointed the same to Jacob for a law, * and to Israel for an everlasting testament:
L.6xr: ^104:11^ Saying: To thee will I give the land of Chanaan, * the lot of your inheritance.
L.6xt: ^104:12^ When they were but a small number: * yea very few, and sojourners therein:
L.6xu: ^104:13^ And they passed from nation to nation, * and from one kingdom to another people.
L.6xw: ^104:14^ He suffered no man to hurt them: * and he reproved kings for their sakes.
L.6xz: ^104:15^ Touch ye not my anointed: * and do no evil to my prophets.
L.6y1: ^104:16^ Et vocávit famem super terram: * et omne firmaméntum panis contrívit.
L.6y3: ^104:17^ Misit ante eos virum: * in servum venúmdatus est Ioseph.
L.6y4: ^104:18^ Humiliavérunt in compédibus pedes eius, ferrum pertránsiit ánimam eius * donec veníret verbum eius.
L.6y6: ^104:19^ Elóquium Dómini inflammávit eum: * misit rex, et solvit eum; princeps populórum, et dimísit eum.
L.6ya: ^104:21^ Constítuit eum dóminum domus suæ: * et príncipem omnis possessiónis suæ:
L.6yd: ^104:22^ Ut erudíret príncipes eius sicut semetípsum: * et senes eius prudéntiam docéret.
L.6yf: ^104:23^ Et intrávit Israël in Ægýptum: * et Iacob áccola fuit in terra Cham.
L.6yh: ^104:24^ Et auxit pópulum suum veheménter: * et firmávit eum super inimícos eius.
L.6yi: ^104:25^ Convértit cor eórum ut odírent pópulum eius: * et dolum fácerent in servos eius.
L.6yl: ^104:26^ Misit Móysen, servum suum: * Aaron, quem elégit ipsum.
L.6yn: ^104:27^ Pósuit in eis verba signórum suórum: * et prodigiórum in terra Cham.
L.6y0: ^104:16^ And he called a famine upon the land: * and he broke in pieces all the support of bread.
L.6y2: ^104:17^ He sent a man before them: * Joseph, who was sold for a slave.
L.6y5: ^104:18^ They humbled his feet in fetters: the iron pierced his soul, * until his word came.
L.6y7: ^104:19^ The word of the Lord inflamed him: * the king sent, and he released him: the ruler of the people, and he set him at liberty.
L.6yb: ^104:21^ He made him master of his house, * and ruler of all his possession.
L.6yc: ^104:22^ That he might instruct his princes as himself, * and teach his ancients wisdom.
L.6ye: ^104:23^ And Israel went into Egypt: * and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Cham.
L.6yg: ^104:24^ And he increased his people exceedingly: * and strengthened them over their enemies,
L.6yj: ^104:25^ He turned their heart to hate his people: * and to deal deceitfully with his servants.
L.6yk: ^104:26^ He sent Moses his servant: * Aaron the man whom he had chosen.
L.6ym: ^104:27^ He gave them power to shew his signs, * and his wonders in the land of Cham.
L.6yp: ^104:28^ Misit ténebras, et obscurávit: * et non exacerbávit sermónes suos.
L.6yq: ^104:29^ Convértit aquas eórum in sánguinem: * et occídit pisces eórum.
L.6yv: ^104:30^ Édidit terra eórum ranas: * in penetrálibus regum ipsórum.
L.6yw: ^104:31^ Dixit, et venit cœnomyía: * et cínifes in ómnibus fínibus eórum.
L.6yz: ^104:32^ Pósuit plúvias eórum grándinem: * ignem comburéntem in terra ipsórum.
L.6z1: ^104:33^ Et percússit víneas eórum, et ficúlneas eórum: * et contrívit lignum fínium eórum.
L.6z2: ^104:34^ Dixit, et venit locústa, et bruchus, * cuius non erat númerus:
L.6z5: ^104:35^ Et comédit omne fænum in terra eórum: * et comédit omnem fructum terræ eórum.
L.6z7: ^104:36^ Et percússit omne primogénitum in terra eórum: * primítias omnis labóris eórum.
L.6z9: ^104:37^ Et edúxit eos cum argénto et auro: * et non erat in tríbubus eórum infírmus.
L.6zb: ^104:38^ Lætáta est Ægýptus in profectióne eórum: * quia incúbuit timor eórum super eos.
L.6zc: ^104:39^ Expándit nubem in protectiónem eórum: * et ignem ut lucéret eis per noctem.
L.6zg: ^104:40^ Petiérunt, et venit cotúrnix: * et pane cæli saturávit eos.
L.6zi: ^104:41^ Dirúpit petram et fluxérunt aquæ: * abiérunt in sicco flúmina;
L.6zl: ^104:42^ Quóniam memor fuit verbi sancti sui: * quod hábuit ad Ábraham, púerum suum.
L.6zn: ^104:43^ Et edúxit pópulum suum in exsultatióne, * et eléctos suos in lætítia.
L.6zp: ^104:44^ Et dedit illis regiónes géntium: * et labóres populórum possedérunt:
L.6zr: ^104:45^ Ut custódiant iustificatiónes eius, * et legem eius requírant.
L.6yo: ^104:28^ He sent darkness, and made it obscure: * and grieved not his words.
L.6yr: ^104:29^ He turned their waters into blood, * and destroyed their fish.
L.6yu: ^104:30^ Their land brought forth frogs, * in the inner chambers of their kings.
L.6yx: ^104:31^ He spoke, and there came diverse sorts of flies, * and sciniphs in all their coasts.
L.6yy: ^104:32^ He gave them hail for rain, * a burning fire in the land.
L.6z0: ^104:33^ And he destroyed their vineyards, and their fig trees: * and he broke in pieces the trees of their coasts.
L.6z3: ^104:34^ He spoke, and the locust came, and the bruchus, * of which there was no number.
L.6z4: ^104:35^ And they devoured all the grass in their land, * and consumed all the fruit of their ground.
L.6z6: ^104:36^ And he slew all the firstborn in their land: * the firstfruits of all their labour.
L.6z8: ^104:37^ And he brought them out with silver and gold: * and there was not among their tribes one that was feeble.
L.6za: ^104:38^ Egypt was glad when they departed: * for the fear of them lay upon them.
L.6zd: ^104:39^ He spread a cloud for their protection, * and fire to give them light in the night.
L.6zh: ^104:40^ They asked, and the quail came: * and he filled them with the bread of heaven.
L.6zj: ^104:41^ He opened the rock, and waters flowed: * rivers ran down in the dry land.
L.6zk: ^104:42^ Because he remembered his holy word, * which he had spoken to his servant Abraham.
L.6zm: ^104:43^ And he brought forth his people with joy, * and his chosen with gladness.
L.6zo: ^104:44^ And he gave them the lands of the Gentiles: * and they possessed the labours of the people:
L.6zq: ^104:45^ That they might observe his justifications, * and seek after his law.
L.81h: ^Ant.^ Surréxit Christus et illúxit pópulo suo, quem redémit sánguine suo, allelúia.
L.81i: ^Ant.^ Surréxit Christus et illúxit pópulo suo, quem redémit sánguine suo, allelúja.
L.7cy: ^17:2^ Díligam te, Dómine, fortitúdo mea: * Dóminus firmaméntum meum, et refúgium meum, et liberátor meus.
L.7dm: ^17:3^ Deus meus adiútor meus, * et sperábo in eum.
L.7dp: ^17:3^ Protéctor meus, et cornu salútis meæ, * et suscéptor meus.
L.7ea: ^17:4^ Laudans invocábo Dóminum: * et ab inimícis meis salvus ero.
L.7eg: ^17:5^ Circumdedérunt me dolóres mortis: * et torréntes iniquitátis conturbavérunt me.
L.7ei: ^17:6^ Dolóres inférni circumdedérunt me: * præoccupavérunt me láquei mortis.
L.7en: ^17:7^ In tribulatióne mea invocávi Dóminum, * et ad Deum meum clamávi.
L.7el: ^17:7^ Et exaudívit de templo sancto suo vocem meam: * et clamor meus in conspéctu eius, introívit in aures eius.
L.7eo: ^17:8^ Commóta est, et contrémuit terra: * fundaménta móntium conturbáta sunt, et commóta sunt, quóniam irátus est eis.
L.7eq: ^17:9^ Ascéndit fumus in ira eius: et ignis a fácie eius exársit: * carbónes succénsi sunt ab eo.
L.7bt: ^17:10^ Inclinávit cælos, et descéndit: * et calígo sub pédibus eius.
L.7bv: ^17:11^ Et ascéndit super Chérubim, et volávit: * volávit super pennas ventórum.
L.7bx: ^17:12^ Et pósuit ténebras latíbulum suum, in circúitu eius tabernáculum eius: * tenebrósa aqua in núbibus áëris.
L.7bz: ^17:13^ Præ fulgóre in conspéctu eius nubes transiérunt, * grando et carbónes ignis.
L.7c1: ^17:14^ Et intónuit de cælo Dóminus, et Altíssimus dedit vocem suam: * grando et carbónes ignis.
L.7c3: ^17:15^ Et misit sagíttas suas, et dissipávit eos: * fúlgura multiplicávit, et conturbávit eos.
L.7c6: ^17:16^ Et apparuérunt fontes aquárum, * et reveláta sunt fundaménta orbis terrárum:
L.7c4: ^17:16^ Ab increpatióne tua, Dómine, * ab inspiratióne spíritus iræ tuæ.
L.7cz: ^17:2^ I will love thee, O Lord, my strength: * The Lord is my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer.
L.7dn: ^17:3^ My God is my helper, * and in him will I put my trust.
L.7do: ^17:3^ My protector, and the horn of my salvation, * and my support.
L.7eb: ^17:4^ Praising, I will call upon the Lord: * and I shall be saved from my enemies.
L.7eh: ^17:5^ The sorrows of death surrounded me: * and the torrents of iniquity troubled me.
L.7ej: ^17:6^ The sorrows of hell encompassed me: * and the snares of death prevented me.
L.7em: ^17:7^ In my affliction I called upon the Lord, * and I cried to my God:
L.7ek: ^17:7^ And he heard my voice from his holy temple: * and my cry before him came into his ears.
L.7ep: ^17:8^ The earth shook and trembled: * the foundations of the mountains were troubled and were moved, because he was angry with them.
L.7er: ^17:9^ There went up a smoke in his wrath: and a fire flamed from his face: * coals were kindled by it.
L.7bs: ^17:10^ He bowed the heavens, and came down, * and darkness was under his feet.
L.7bu: ^17:11^ And he ascended upon the cherubim, and he flew; * he flew upon the wings of the winds.
L.7bw: ^17:12^ And he made darkness his covert, his pavilion round about him: * dark waters in the clouds of the air.
L.7by: ^17:13^ At the brightness that was before him the clouds passed, * hail and coals of fire.
L.7c0: ^17:14^ And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Highest gave his voice: * hail and coals of fire.
L.7c2: ^17:15^ And he sent forth his arrows, and he scattered them: * he multiplied lightnings, and troubled them.
L.7c7: ^17:16^ Then the fountains of waters appeared, * and the foundations of the world were discovered:
L.7c5: ^17:16^ At thy rebuke, O Lord, * at the blast of the spirit of thy wrath.
L.7c9: ^17:17^ Misit de summo, et accépit me: * et assúmpsit me de aquis multis.
L.7ca: ^17:18^ Erípuit me de inimícis meis fortíssimis, et ab his qui odérunt me: * quóniam confortáti sunt super me.
L.7cc: ^17:19^ Prævenérunt me in die afflictiónis meæ: * et factus est Dóminus protéctor meus.
L.7cf: ^17:20^ Et edúxit me in latitúdinem: * salvum me fecit, quóniam vóluit me.
L.7ch: ^17:21^ Et retríbuet mihi Dóminus secúndum iustítiam meam: * et secúndum puritátem mánuum meárum retríbuet mihi:
L.7cj: ^17:22^ Quia custodívi vias Dómini, * nec ímpie gessi a Deo meo.
L.7cl: ^17:23^ Quóniam ómnia iudícia eius in conspéctu meo: * et iustítias eius non répuli a me.
L.7cn: ^17:24^ Et ero immaculátus cum eo: * et observábo me ab iniquitáte mea.
L.7cp: ^17:25^ Et retríbuet mihi Dóminus secúndum iustítiam meam: * et secúndum puritátem mánuum meárum in conspéctu oculórum eius.
L.7cq: ^17:26^ Cum sancto sanctus eris, * et cum viro innocénte ínnocens eris:
L.7ct: ^17:27^ Et cum elécto eléctus eris: * et cum pervérso pervertéris.
L.7cv: ^17:28^ Quóniam tu pópulum húmilem salvum fácies: * et óculos superbórum humiliábis.
L.7cx: ^17:29^ Quóniam tu illúminas lucérnam meam, Dómine: * Deus meus, illúmina ténebras meas.
L.7d1: ^17:30^ Quóniam in te erípiar a tentatióne, * et in Deo meo transgrédiar murum.
L.7d3: ^17:31^ Deus meus, impollúta via eius: elóquia Dómini igne examináta: * protéctor est ómnium sperántium in se.
L.7d5: ^17:32^ Quóniam quis Deus præter Dóminum? * aut quis Deus præter Deum nostrum?
L.7d6: ^17:33^ Deus, qui præcínxit me virtúte: * et pósuit immaculátam viam meam.
L.7d8: ^17:34^ Qui perfécit pedes meos tamquam cervórum, * et super excélsa státuens me.
L.7da: ^17:35^ Qui docet manus meas ad prǽlium: * et posuísti, ut arcum ǽreum, brácchia mea.
L.7c8: ^17:17^ He sent from on high, and took me: * and received me out of many waters.
L.7cb: ^17:18^ He delivered me from my strongest enemies, and from them that hated me: * for they were too strong for me.
L.7cd: ^17:19^ They prevented me in the day of my affliction: * and the Lord became my protector.
L.7ce: ^17:20^ And he brought me forth into a large place: * he saved me, because he was well pleased with me.
L.7cg: ^17:21^ And the Lord will reward me according to my justice; * and will repay me according to the cleanness of my hands:
L.7ci: ^17:22^ Because I have kept the ways of the Lord; * and have not done wickedly against my God.
L.7ck: ^17:23^ For all his judgments are in my sight: * and his justices I have not put away from me.
L.7cm: ^17:24^ And I shall be spotless with him: * and shall keep myself from my iniquity.
L.7co: ^17:25^ And the Lord will reward me according to my justice: * and according to the cleanness of my hands before his eyes.
L.7cr: ^17:26^ With the holy thou wilt be holy; * and with the innocent man thou wilt be innocent:
L.7cs: ^17:27^ And with the elect thou wilt be elect: * and with the perverse thou wilt be perverted.
L.7cu: ^17:28^ For thou wilt save the humble people; * but wilt bring down the eyes of the proud.
L.7cw: ^17:29^ For thou lightest my lamp, O Lord: * O my God, enlighten my darkness.
L.7d0: ^17:30^ For by thee I shall be delivered from temptation; * and through my God I shall go over a wall.
L.7d2: ^17:31^ As for my God, his way is undefiled: the words of the Lord are fire-tried: * he is the protector of all that trust in him.
L.7d4: ^17:32^ For who is God but the Lord? * or who is God but our God?
L.7d7: ^17:33^ God, who hath girt me with strength; * and made my way blameless.
L.7d9: ^17:34^ Who hath made my feet like the feet of harts: * and who setteth me upon high places.
L.7db: ^17:35^ Who teacheth my hands to war: * and thou hast made my arms like a brazen bow.
L.7dd: ^17:36^ Et dedísti mihi protectiónem salútis tuæ: * et déxtera tua suscépit me:
L.7de: ^17:36^ Et disciplína tua corréxit me in finem: * et disciplína tua ipsa me docébit.
L.7dg: ^17:37^ Dilatásti gressus meos subtus me: * et non sunt infirmáta vestígia mea:
L.7dj: ^17:38^ Pérsequar inimícos meos et comprehéndam illos: * et non convértar, donec defíciant.
L.7dk: ^17:39^ Confríngam illos, nec póterunt stare: * cadent subtus pedes meos.
L.7dr: ^17:40^ Et præcinxísti me virtúte ad bellum: * et supplantásti insurgéntes in me subtus me.
L.7dt: ^17:41^ Et inimícos meos dedísti mihi dorsum, * et odiéntes me disperdidísti.
L.7du: ^17:42^ Clamavérunt, nec erat qui salvos fáceret ad Dóminum: * nec exaudívit eos.
L.7dx: ^17:43^ Et commínuam eos, ut púlverem ante fáciem venti: * ut lutum plateárum delébo eos.
L.7dy: ^17:44^ Erípies me de contradictiónibus pópuli: * constítues me in caput géntium.
L.7e1: ^17:45^ Pópulus quem non cognóvi servívit mihi: * in audítu auris obedívit mihi.
L.7e2: ^17:46^ Fílii aliéni mentíti sunt mihi, * fílii aliéni inveteráti sunt, et claudicavérunt a sémitis suis.
L.7e5: ^17:47^ Vivit Dóminus, et benedíctus Deus meus: * et exaltétur Deus salútis meæ.
L.7e6: ^17:48^ Deus, qui das vindíctas mihi, et subdis pópulos sub me: * liberátor meus de inimícis meis iracúndis.
L.7e9: ^17:49^ Et ab insurgéntibus in me exaltábis me: * a viro iníquo erípies me.
L.7ec: ^17:50^ Proptérea confitébor tibi in natiónibus, Dómine: * et nómini tuo psalmum dicam.
L.7ef: ^17:51^ Magníficans salútes Regis eius, et fáciens misericórdiam Christo suo David: * et sémini eius usque in sǽculum.
L.7df: ^17:36^ Thou hast given me the protection of thy salvation: * and thy right hand hath held me up:
L.7dc: ^17:36^ And thy discipline hath corrected me unto the end: * and thy discipline, the same shall teach me.
L.7dh: ^17:37^ Thou hast enlarged my steps under me; * and my feet are not weakened.
L.7di: ^17:38^ I will pursue after my enemies, and overtake them: * and I will not turn again till they are consumed.
L.7dl: ^17:39^ I will break them, and they shall not be able to stand: * they shall fall under my feet.
L.7dq: ^17:40^ And thou hast girded me with strength unto battle; * and hast subdued under me them that rose up against me.
L.7ds: ^17:41^ And thou hast made my enemies turn their back upon me, * and hast destroyed them that hated me.
L.7dv: ^17:42^ They cried, but there was none to save them, to the Lord: * but he heard them not.
L.7dw: ^17:43^ And I shall beat them as small as the dust before the wind; * I shall bring them to nought, like the dirt in the streets.
L.7dz: ^17:44^ Thou wilt deliver me from the contradictions of the people; * thou wilt make me head of the Gentiles.
L.7e0: ^17:45^ A people which I knew not, hath served me: * at the hearing of the ear they have obeyed me.
L.7e3: ^17:46^ The children that are strangers have lied to me, * strange children have faded away, and have halted from their paths.
L.7e4: ^17:47^ The Lord liveth, and blessed be my God, * and let the God of my salvation be exalted.
L.7e7: ^17:48^ O God, who avengest me, and subduest the people under me, * my deliverer from my enraged enemies.
L.7e8: ^17:49^ And thou wilt lift me up above them that rise up against me: * from the unjust man thou wilt deliver me.
L.7ed: ^17:50^ Therefore will I give glory to thee, O Lord, among the nations, * and I will sing a psalm to thy name.
L.7ee: ^17:51^ Giving great deliverance to his king, and shewing mercy to David, his anointed: * and to his seed for ever.
L.7jw: ^36:1^ Noli æmulári in malignántibus: * neque zeláveris faciéntes iniquitátem.
L.7km: ^36:2^ Quóniam tamquam fænum velóciter aréscent: * et quemádmodum ólera herbárum cito décident.
L.7l7: ^36:3^ Spera in Dómino, et fac bonitátem: * et inhábita terram, et pascéris in divítiis eius.
L.7ld: ^36:4^ Delectáre in Dómino: * et dabit tibi petitiónes cordis tui.
L.7lj: ^36:5^ Revéla Dómino viam tuam, et spera in eo: * et ipse fáciet.
L.7lm: ^36:6^ Et edúcet quasi lumen iustítiam tuam: et iudícium tuum tamquam merídiem: * súbditus esto Dómino, et ora eum.
L.7lq: ^36:7^ Noli æmulári in eo, qui prosperátur in via sua: * in hómine faciénte iniustítias.
L.7lu: ^36:8^ Désine ab ira, et derelínque furórem: * noli æmulári ut malignéris.
L.7m0: ^36:9^ Quóniam qui malignántur, exterminabúntur: * sustinéntes autem Dóminum, ipsi hereditábunt terram.
L.7it: ^36:10^ Et adhuc pusíllum, et non erit peccátor: * et quæres locum eius et non invénies.
L.7j0: ^36:11^ Mansuéti autem hereditábunt terram: * et delectabúntur in multitúdine pacis.
L.7j3: ^36:12^ Observábit peccátor iustum: * et stridébit super eum déntibus suis.
L.7j7: ^36:13^ Dóminus autem irridébit eum: * quóniam próspicit quod véniet dies eius.
L.7j9: ^36:14^ Gládium evaginavérunt peccatóres: * intendérunt arcum suum,
L.7je: ^36:14^ Ut deíciant páuperem et ínopem: * ut trucídent rectos corde.
L.7jf: ^36:15^ Gládius eórum intret in corda ipsórum: * et arcus eórum confringátur.
L.7jt: ^36:1^ Be not emulous of evildoers; * nor envy them that work iniquity.
L.7kl: ^36:2^ For they shall shortly wither away as grass, * and as the green herbs shall quickly fall.
L.7l9: ^36:3^ Trust in the Lord, and do good, * and dwell in the land, and thou shalt be fed with its riches.
L.7le: ^36:4^ Delight in the Lord, * and he will give thee the requests of thy heart.
L.7lh: ^36:5^ Commit thy way to the Lord, and trust in him, * and he will do it.
L.7ll: ^36:6^ And he will bring forth thy justice as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday: * be subject to the Lord and pray to him.
L.7lp: ^36:7^ Envy not the man who prospereth in his way; * the man who doth unjust things.
L.7lt: ^36:8^ Cease from anger, and leave rage; * have no emulation to do evil.
L.7ly: ^36:9^ For the evildoers shall be cut off: * but they that wait upon the Lord shall inherit the land.
L.7iu: ^36:10^ For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: * and thou shalt seek his place, and shalt not find it.
L.7ix: ^36:11^ But the meek shall inherit the land, * and shall delight in abundance of peace.
L.7j4: ^36:12^ The sinner shall watch the just man: * and shall gnash upon him with his teeth.
L.7j6: ^36:13^ But the Lord shall laugh at him: * for he foreseeth that his day shall come.
L.7jc: ^36:14^ The wicked have drawn out the sword: * they have bent their bow.
L.7jd: ^36:14^ To cast down the poor and needy, * to kill the upright of heart.
L.7jh: ^36:15^ Let their sword enter into their own hearts, * and let their bow be broken.
L.7jl: ^36:16^ Mélius est módicum iusto, * super divítias peccatórum multas.
L.7jo: ^36:17^ Quóniam brácchia peccatórum conteréntur: * confírmat autem iustos Dóminus.
L.7jp: ^36:18^ Novit Dóminus dies immaculatórum: * et heréditas eórum in ætérnum erit.
L.7jr: ^36:19^ Non confundéntur in témpore malo, et in diébus famis saturabúntur: * quia peccatóres períbunt.
L.7jy: ^36:20^ Inimíci vero Dómini mox ut honorificáti fúerint et exaltáti: * deficiéntes, quemádmodum fumus defícient.
L.7jz: ^36:21^ Mutuábitur peccátor, et non solvet: * iustus autem miserétur et tríbuet.
L.7k2: ^36:22^ Quia benedicéntes ei hereditábunt terram: * maledicéntes autem ei disperíbunt.
L.7k3: ^36:23^ Apud Dóminum gressus hóminis dirigéntur: * et viam eius volet.
L.7k5: ^36:24^ Cum cecíderit non collidétur: * quia Dóminus suppónit manum suam.
L.7k8: ^36:25^ Iúnior fui, étenim sénui: * et non vidi iustum derelíctum, nec semen eius quærens panem.
L.7ka: ^36:26^ Tota die miserétur et cómmodat: * et semen illíus in benedictióne erit.
L.7kc: ^36:27^ Declína a malo, et fac bonum: * et inhábita in sǽculum sǽculi.
L.7kf: ^36:28^ Quia Dóminus amat iudícium, et non derelínquet sanctos suos: * in ætérnum conservabúntur.
L.7ke: ^36:28^ Iniústi puniéntur: * et semen impiórum períbit.
L.7ki: ^36:29^ Iusti autem hereditábunt terram: * et inhabitábunt in sǽculum sǽculi super eam.
L.7jj: ^36:16^ Better is a little to the just, * than the great riches of the wicked.
L.7jn: ^36:17^ For the arms of the wicked shall be broken in pieces; * but the Lord strengtheneth the just.
L.7jq: ^36:18^ The Lord knoweth the days of the undefiled; * and their inheritance shall be for ever.
L.7js: ^36:19^ They shall not be confounded in the evil time; and in the days of famine they shall be filled, * because the wicked shall perish.
L.7jx: ^36:20^ And the enemies of the Lord, presently after they shall be honoured and exalted, * shall come to nothing and vanish like smoke.
L.7k0: ^36:21^ The sinner shall borrow, and not pay again; * but the just sheweth mercy and shall give.
L.7k1: ^36:22^ For such as bless him shall inherit the land: * but such as curse him shall perish.
L.7k4: ^36:23^ With the Lord shall the steps of a man be directed, * and he shall like well his way.
L.7k6: ^36:24^ When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, * for the Lord putteth his hand under him.
L.7k7: ^36:25^ I have been young, and now am old; * and I have not seen the just forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread.
L.7k9: ^36:26^ He sheweth mercy, and lendeth all the day long; * and his seed shall be in blessing.
L.7kb: ^36:27^ Decline from evil and do good, * and dwell for ever and ever.
L.7kd: ^36:28^ For the Lord loveth judgment, and will not forsake his saints: * they shall be preserved for ever.

L.7ns: ^48:12^ Their dwelling places to all generations: * they have called their lands by their names.

L.7nw: ^48:14^ This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them: * and afterwards they shall delight in their mouth.
L.7o0: ^48:15^ They are laid in hell like sheep: * death shall feed upon them.
L.7nx: ^48:15^ And the just shall have dominion over them in the morning; * and their help shall decay in hell from their glory.

L.aba: In illo témpore: Dixit Iesus discípulis suis: Módicum, et iam non vidébitis me; et íterum módicum, et vidébitis me: quia vado ad Patrem. Et réliqua.
L.ar8: Módicum est hoc totum spátium, quo præsens pérvolat sǽculum. Unde dicit idem ipse Evangelísta in Epístola sua: Novíssima hora est. Ideo namque áddidit: Quia vado ad Patrem: quod ad priórem senténtiam referéndum est, ubi ait: Módicum et iam non vidébitis me: non ad posteriórem, ubi ait: Et íterum módicum, et vidébitis me. Eúndo quippe ad Patrem, factúrus erat ut eum non vidérent.
L.fs5: ^℟.^ Dignus es, Dómine, accípere librum, et aperíre signácula eius, allelúia: quóniam occísus es, et redemísti nos Deo
L.975: At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: A little while, and now you shall not see me; and again a little while, and you shall see me: because I go to the Father. And so on.
L.bl7: This little while is the whole duration of this present world. In the same sense this same Evangelist saith in his Epistle ^ii. 18^: It is the last time. The words, because I go to the Father, refer to the first clause of the text, namely, A little while and ye shall not see Me, and not to the latter clause, that is, and again a little while, and ye shall see Me. By His going to the Father He was about to bring it to pass that they should see Him no more.
L.a7m: Illis ergo ait: Módicum, et iam non vidébitis me; qui eum corporáliter tunc vidébant: quia itúrus erat ad Patrem, et eum deínceps mortálem visúri non erant, qualem, cum ista loquerétur, vidébant. Quod vero áddidit: Et íterum módicum, et vidébitis me: univérsæ promísit Ecclésiæ, sicut univérsæ promísit: Ecce ego vobíscum sum usque ad consummatiónem sǽculi. Non tardat Dóminus promíssum.
L.fth: ^℟.^ Ego sicut vitis fructificávi suavitátem odóris, allelúia:
L.8xt: * Transíte ad me, omnes qui concupíscitis me, et a generatiónibus meis adimplémini, allelúia, allelúia.
L.gre: ^℣.^ Ego diligéntes me díligo; et qui mane vigiláverint ad me, invénient me.

L.a2s: He saith: A little while, and ye shall not see Me, a little while, and they who now saw Him clad in a dying nature, should see Him so no more, because He was about to go to the Father. But He saith: And again a little while, and ye shall see Me, and these words are a promise to the Universal Church, just as are those others: Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world ^Matth. xxviii. 20.^ Our Lord delayeth not His promised coming.

L.ar9: Módicum et vidébimus eum: ubi iam nihil rogémus, nihil interrogémus, quia nihil desiderándum remanébit, nihil quæréndum latébit. Hoc módicum longum nobis vidétur, quóniam adhuc ágitur; cum finítum fúerit, tunc sentiémus quam módicum fúerit. Non ergo sit gáudium nostrum quale habet mundus, de quo dictum est: Mundus autem gaudébit. Nec tamen in huius desidérii parturitióne sine gáudio tristes simus: sed, sicut ait Apóstolus: Spe gaudéntes.

L.91d: Again a little while, and we shall see Him. We shall see Him. And, O, when we shall see Him, then we shall beg, we shall ask no more; for no desire will be unsatisfied, and no riddle unsolved. This little while seemeth a very long while to us now, while as it is still going on, but when it is over we shall feel indeed how truly it is but a little while. Therefore, may our rejoicing never be like the rejoicing of that world whereof it is said: The world shall rejoice..

L.nv2: The Church, most provident Mother of All, expends the greatest efforts for the protection and relief of the workers, erecting and promoting for them societies which Pius XII, the Supreme Pontiff, now wishes to be entrusted to the most powerful patronage of St. Joseph. For St. Joseph, since he was reckoned the father of Christ, who deigned to be called the son of a workman, on account of the irrevocable bond which united him to Jesus, drank abundantly of that spirit which ennobles and elevates labor. In like manner, associations of workers ought to be aware of the same kind of spirit, so that Christ may always be present in them, in their members, in their families and in fact in every labor organization, because the chief purpose of these associations is to foster and nourish the Christian life in their members, to spread the Kingdom of God more widely, especially among fellow workers in the same plant.

L.nzc: The same Pontiff supplied a new proof of the Church's solicitude for labor organization, when, upon the occasion of a convention of workingmen held in Rome on the first of May in the year 1955, he took the opportunity of speaking to a large multitude gathered in the square before St. Peter's Basilica, and commended most highly the instruction of workingmen. For in our day it is of prime importance that the workers be properly imbued with Christian doctrine in order that they may avoid the widespread errors concerning the nature of society and economic matters. Moreover, such instruction is needed that they might have a correct knowledge of the moral order established by God as it effects the rights and duties of workers, and which the Church discloses and interprets, so that by partaking in the needed reforms they might work more effectively toward their realization. L.kti: In order that the dignity of human labor and the principles which underlie it might penetrate more deeply into souls, Pius XII has instituted the feast of St. Joseph the Workman, as an example and a protection for all associations of workers. For from this example, those who follow the worker's calling ought to learn how and in what spirit they should discharge their duties, so that, obeying the first law of God, they might likewise subdue the earth and attain to economic prosperity, and at the same time reap the rewards of eternal life. Nor will the prudent guardian of the Family of Nazareth fail to shield with his protection, and from heaven bless the homes of those who, like him, are artisans and workmen. Most aptly has the Supreme Pontiff ordered this feast to be celebrated on the first of May, a day which the workers have adopted as their own; from henceforth let it be hoped that this day, dedicated to St. Joseph the Workman, will, as time goes on, not sharpen hatred and inflame strife, but with each recurring year, invite everyone to strive more and more for those things which are still lacking to civil peace, and indeed that it may stimulate the public authorities to use their abilities in effecting whatever right order demands of human fellowship.

L.mfc: On the Sabbath day he entered the synagogue, where those who came to listen had gathered. And the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were intent upon him. Some indeed with devotion, some out of curiosity, while some watched him that they might trap him in his talk. And the Scribes and Pharisees said to the people, in whom faith and devotion had already made a beginning: “Is not this the son of Joseph?” See this attitude of disparagement toward him whom they did not even deign to call by his name. “The son of Joseph,” this little the Evangelist says because he had known that both in Mark and in Matthew a fuller statement would be made: “Is not this the carpenter's son? Is he not a workman, the son of Mary?” All these things were said contemptuously.

Num et Saul inter prophétas est? » Parva ergo locútio magnum impórtat despéctum. Dóminus autem dixit: « Amen dico vobis, quia nemo prophéta accéptus est in pátria sua. » Se autem prophétam hic dicit Dóminus. Ipse enim, cui ómnia per divinitátem nota sunt, nullam pénitus récipit inspiratiónis revelatiónem. Pátriam autem suam vocat hic stricte locum conceptiónis et nutritiónis. Suis autem convicáneis, qui invídia incitabántur ad ipsum, non fuit accéptus.
L.m0h: Now the Lord was a workman because the prophet said of him: “You fashioned the moon and the sun.” A similar contemptuous way of speaking is found in the Book of Kings, where they said of Saul when he became king: “What is this that has happened to the son of Cis? Is Saul also among the prophets?” This slight remark shows great disparagement. For the Lord says: “Amen I say to you, that no prophet is acceptable in his own country.” Here the Lord calls himself a prophet. For he, to whom all things are known through his divinity, receives no revelation of inspiration from outside himself. Here, however, he definitely calls the place of his birth and upbringing his own country. But he was not acceptable to his fellow townsmen who were incited against him by envy.

L.ohu: We have now to consider these words of the Lord “Amen, Amen, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in My Name, He will give it you.” It hath already been said in the earlier part of this discourse of the Lord, for the sake of some who ask the Father in Christ's Name and receive not, that whatsoever is asked, which tendeth not to salvation, is not asked in the Name of the Saviour. By the words “In My Name” we must not understand the vocalization of letters and syllables, but the meaning of what is said, the honest and true meaning.
L.oaa: Unde qui hoc sentit de Christo, quod non est de único Dei Fílio sentiéndum, non petit in eius nómine, etiámsi non táceat lítteris ac sýllabis Christum: quóniam in eius nómine petit, quem cógitat cum petit. Qui vero quod est de illo sentiéndum sentit, ipse in eius nómine petit: et áccipit quod petit, si non contra suam salútem sempitérnam petit. Accipit autem quando debet accípere. Quædam enim non negántur: sed ut cóngruo dentur témpore differúntur.
L.o0w: Therefore, whosoever thinketh of Christ as he ought not to think of the Only Son of God, such an one doth not ask anything in Christ's Name, although he do actually utter letters and syllables to that effect, because by these sounds he meaneth not the Real Christ, but a fancied being who hath no existence except in the speaker's imagination. But on the other hand, whosoever thinketh of Christ as he ought to think, the same asketh in Christ's Name, and receiveth, provided only it be nothing against his own everlasting salvation but if it is good for him to receive, he receiveth. Some things are not given at once, but kept over till a more fitting season. Such is the true interpretation of the words “He will give it you” namely, that those things will be given which are good for them to ask. All the Saints also are heard when they ask for themselves, but not necessarily when they ask for their friends, or their enemies, or others, even as it is written, not simply “He will give it” but “He will give it you.”
L.l10: Ita sane intelligéndum est quod ait: Dabit vobis: ut ea benefícia significáta sciántur his verbis, quæ ad eos, qui petunt, próprie pértinent. Exaudiúntur quippe omnes Sancti pro seípsis, non autem pro ómnibus exaudiúntur vel amícis, vel inimícis suis, vel quibúslibet áliis: quia non utcúmque dictum est, Dabit; sed, Dabit vobis. Usque modo, inquit, non petístis quidquam in nómine meo. Pétite, et accipiétis, ut gáudium vestrum sit plenum. Hoc quod dicit, gáudium plenum, profécto non carnále, sed spiritále gáudium est.
L.o0x: Therefore, whosoever thinketh of Christ as he ought not to think of the Only Son of God, such an one doth not ask anything in Christ's Name, although he do actually utter letters and syllables to that effect, because by these sounds he meaneth not the Real Christ, but a fancied being who hath no existence except in the speaker's imagination. But on the other hand, whosoever thinketh of Christ as he ought to think, the same asketh in Christ's Name, and receiveth, provided only it be nothing against his own everlasting salvation but if it is good for him to receive, he receiveth. Some things are not given at once, but kept over till a more fitting season. Such is the true interpretation of the words “He will give it you” namely, that those things will be given which are good for them to ask. All the Saints also are heard when they ask for themselves, but not necessarily when they ask for their friends, or their enemies, or others, even as it is written, not simply “He will give it” but “He will give it you.” Hitherto saith the Lord, have ye asked nothing in My Name? “Ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full.” This their joy, whereof He saith that it shall be full, is to be understood not of fleshly but of spiritual joy and when that joy is so great that it can be increased no more, then shall it without doubt be full. Whatsoever therefore we ask for the fulfilling of this joy, (that is, if we thereby mean grace, if we ask for that life which is the really blessed one,) that is a thing which it is meet to ask in Christ's Name. If we ask anything else than this, we ask nothing, although we do actually ask something, because all things are nothing in comparison with this.

L.lqb: Monica, the devout mother of St. Augustine and a shining example to wives and mothers, followed her son to Milan when he become a Manichaean and, by her constant prayers, tears and fasting, gained him for Christ with the help of Ambrose the bishop. When she was returning with him to Africa, she fell ill of fever at Ostia on the Tiber, and, after nine days, died peacefully. After telling about her death, her sorrowing son adds: We did not think that hers was a death which it was seemly to mark with repining, or tears, or lamentations, seeing that she died not sorrowfully, nor at all as touching her best and noblest part. This we knew, because we knew what her life had been, her faith unfeigned, her sure and certain hope. And then, nevertheless, I remembered again what thine handmaid was used to be, her walk with thee, how godly and holy it was, and with us so gentle and long-suffering; and that it was all gone away from me now. And I wept, over her and for her. And if any man will make it blame to me that I wept for a little while, when I saw lying dead before mine eyes my mother, who had wept over me so many years, that she might see me live, I say, if any man will make it blame to me, I pray him not to sneer at me, but rather (if his charity be so great) himself to weep over my sins before thee, who art a Father to all them to whom thy Christ is a Brother. St. Monica's body was first buried in the Church of St. Aurea, but, long after, in the papacy of Martin V, it was carried to Rome and honourably buried again in the Church of St. Augustine.

L.kiw: I may be allowed to say that the disciples' slowness to believe that the Lord had indeed risen from the dead, was not so much their weakness as our strength. In consequence of their doubts, the fact of the Resurrection was demonstrated by many infallible proofs. These proofs we read and acknowledge. What then assureth our faith, if not their doubt? For my part, I put my trust in Thomas, who doubted long, much more than in Mary Magdalene, who believed at once. Through his doubting, he came actually to handle the holes of the Wounds, and thereby closed up any wound of doubt in our hearts.

L.m0a: Now confirm to our minds the trustworthiness of the fact that our Lord did indeed rise again from the dead, it is well for us to remark one of the statements of Luke ^Acts i. 4.^ “Eating together with them, He commanded them that they should not ^1 John xiv. 16, 17 xvi. 7.^ depart from Jerusalem and a little afterward: “While they beheld, He was taken up, and a cloud received Him out of their sight.” Consider these words, note well these mysteries. After “eating together with them He was taken up.” He ate and ascended: that the fact of His eating might show the reality of the Body in Which He went up. But Mark telleth us that before the Lord ascended into heaven, He upbraided His disciples; with their unbelief and hardness of heart. From this I know not why we should gather, but that the Lord then upbraided His disciples, for whom He was about to be parted in the body, to the end that the words which He spoke unto them as He left them might be the deeper imprinted on their hearts.

L.okl: When then, He had rebuked the hardness of their heart, what command did He give them? Let us hear. “Go ye into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.” Was the Holy Gospel, then my brethren, to be preached to thing insensate, or to brute beasts, that the Lord said to His disciples: “Preach the Gospel to every creature”? Nay, but by the words “every creature” we must understand man, in whom are combined qualities of all creatures. Being he hath in common with stones, life in common with trees, feeling in common with beasts, understanding in common with angels. If, then, man hath something in common with every creature, man is to a certain extent every creature. The Gospel, then, if it be preached to man only, is preached to every creature.

Sed, Deo áliter disponénte, canónicus Cracoviénsis et concionátor factus a Lampérto epíscopo, in eius póstea locum, quamvis invítus, sufféctus est. Quo in múnere ómnium pastorálium virtútum laude, et præcípue misericórdia in páuperes enítuit. Bolesláum Polóniæ regem, sǽpius ob mores corrúptos frustra admónitum, a fidélium communióne remóvit. Qui idcírco iracúndia furens, mílites in ecclésiam immíttit, ut sanctum epíscopum confódiant; sed cum divínitus fuíssent depúlsi, ímpius rex sacerdótem Dei, Hóstiam immaculátam ad altáre offeréntem, sua manu obtrúncat. L.nmi: Stanislas was born of a noble family at Krakow. His birth was God's answer to the devout prayers of his parents, who in thirty years of marriage had remained childless. From his earliest days, he gave tokens of future holiness, and, as a young man, made great progress in the study of canon law and theology. When his parents died, he distributed his large inheritance to the poor, intending to embrace the monastic life. But God arranged otherwise, and he was made Canon and Preacher in Krakow by Bishop Lampert. Against his wishes, he later became Bishop Lampert's successor, and in this office he was a shining example of every pastoral virtue, especially of kindness to the poor. He excommunicated Boleslas, King of Poland, whom he had often rebuked in vain for his corrupt way of life. In a violent rage the King sent soldiers to the church to kill the holy Bishop. But when these were driven off by the power of God, the King with his own hand beheaded Bishop Stanislas as he was offering the immaculate Victim on the altar. God proclaimed the holiness of his servant by many miracles after his death; and on the strength of them Innocent IV enrolled him among the Saints.

Quam vero Christus eum familiáriter adhibéret, illud fácile declárat, quod gentíles Salvatórem vidére cupiéntes, ad Philíppum accessérunt; et Dóminus, cum in solitúdine hóminum multitúdinem páscere vellet, sic Philíppum affátus est: Unde emémus panes, ut mandúcent hi? Is, accépto Spíritu Sancto, cum ei Scýthia ad prædicándum Evangélium obtigísset, omnem fere illam gentem ad christiánam fidem convértit. Postrémo, cum Hierápolim Phrýgiæ venísset, pro Christi nómine cruci affíxus lapidibúsque óbrutus est. Eius corpus ibídem a Christiánis sepúltum, póstea Romam delátum, in basílica duódecim Apostolórum una cum córpore beáti Iacóbi Apóstoli cónditum est.
L.8td: * Isti sunt viri sancti facti amíci Dei, allelúia.
L.g2y: ^℟.^ Isti sunt viri sancti facti amíci Dei, allelúia.
L.mk7: Philip was born in the town of Bethsaida, and was one of the first of the twelve Apostles who were called by the Lord Christ. Then Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him: “We have found Him of Whom Moses in the Law, and the Prophets, did write.” And so he brought him to the Lord. How familiarly he was in the company of Christ, is manifest from that which is written: “There were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the Feast the same came therefore to Philip, and desired him, saying: Sir, we would see Jesus.” When the Lord was in the wilderness, and was about to feed a great multitude, He said unto Philip: “Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” Philip, after that he had received the Holy Ghost, took Scythia, by lot, as the land wherein he was to preach the Gospel, and brought nearly all that people to believe in Christ. At the last he came to Hierapolis in Phrygia, and there, for Christ’s Name’s sake, he was fastened to a cross and stoned to death. The Christians of Hierapolis buried his body at that place, but it was afterwards brought to Rome and laid in the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, beside that of the blessed Apostle James.
L.8xe: * These men are holy, for they are the friends of God, alleluia.
L.gek: ^℟.^ These men are holy, for they are the friends of God, alleluia.
L.kjp: Iacóbus frater Dómini, cognoménto Iustus, ab ineúnte ætáte vinum et síceram non bibit, carne abstínuit, nunquam tonsus est, nec unguénto nec bálneo usus. Huic uni licébat íngredi in Sancta sanctórum. Idem líneis véstibus utebátur: cui étiam assidúitas orándi ita callum génibus obdúxerat, ut durítie caméli pellem imitarétur. Eum post Christi ascensiónem Apóstoli Ierosolymórum epíscopum creavérunt; ad quem étiam Princeps Apostolórum misit qui nuntiáret se e cárcere ab Angelo edúctum fuísse. Cum autem in concílio Ierosólymis controvérsia esset orta de lege et circumcisióne; Iacóbus, Petri senténtiam secútus, ad fratres hábuit conciónem, in qua vocatiónem géntium probávit, fratribúsque abséntibus scribéndum esse dixit, ne géntibus iugum Mosáicæ legis impónerent. De quo et lóquitur Apóstolus ad Gálatas: Alium autem Apostolórum vidi néminem, nisi Iacóbum fratrem Dómini.
L.8u2: * Modo coronántur, et accípiunt palmam, allelúia.
L.g4p: ^℟.^ Modo coronántur, et accípiunt palmam, allelúia.
L.l1u: James, surnamed the Just, the brother of our Lord Jesus Christ, was a Nazarite from the womb. During his whole life he never drank wine or strong drink, never ate meat, never shaved, and never took a bath. He was the only man who was allowed to go into the Holy of Holies. His raiment was always linen. So continually did he kneel in prayer, that the skin of his knees became horny, like a camel’s knees. After Christ was ascended, the Apostles made James Bishop of Jerusalem and even the Prince of the Apostles gave special intelligence to him after that he was delivered from prison by an angel. When in the Council of Jerusalem certain questions were mooted touching the law and circumcision, James, following the opinion of Peter, addressed a discourse to the brethren, wherein he proved the call of the Gentiles, and commanded letters to be sent to such brethren as were absent, that they might take heed not to lay upon the Gentiles the yoke of the Law of Moses. It is of him that the Apostle Paul saith, writing to the Galatians: “Other of the Apostles saw I none, save James the Lord’s brother.”
L.8my: * And now have they crowns on their heads, and palms in their hands, alleluia.
L.fmr: ^℟.^ And now have they crowns on their heads, and palms in their hands, alleluia.
L.nrp: Tanta autem erat Iacóbi vitæ sánctitas, ut fímbriam vestiménti eius certátim hómines cúperent attíngere. Nam is nonagínta sex annos natus, cum trigínta annis illi Ecclésiæ sanctíssime præfuísset, Christum Dei Fílium constantíssime prǽdicans, lapídibus primum appétitur; mox in altíssimum Templi locum addúctus, inde præcipitátus est. Qui, confráctis crúribus, iacens semivívus, manus tendébat ad cælum, Deúmque pro illórum salúte deprecabátur his verbis: Ignósce eis, Dómine, quia nésciunt quid fáciunt. Qua in oratióne, gráviter eius cápite fullónis fuste percússo, ánimam Deo réddidit, séptimo Nerónis anno, et iuxta Templum, ubi præcipitátus fúerat, sepúltus est. Unam scripsit Epístolam, quæ de septem cathólicis est.
L.8vf: * Qui in patiéntia vestra possidébitis ánimas vestras, allelúia.
L.g8o: ^℟.^ Qui in patiéntia vestra possidébitis ánimas vestras, allelúia.
L.njy: So great was James’ holiness of life that men strove one with another to touch the hem of his garment. When he was ninety-six years old, and had most holily governed the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years, ever most constantly preaching Christ the Son of God, he laid down his life for the faith. He was first stoned, and afterward taken up on to a pinnacle of the Temple and cast down from thence. His legs were broken by the fall, and he was well-nigh dead, but he lifted up his hands towards heaven, and prayed to God for the salvation of his murderers, saying: “Lord, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” As he said this, one that stood by smote him grievously upon the head with a fuller’s club, and he resigned his spirit to God. He testified in the seventh year of Nero, and was buried hard by the Temple, in the place where he had fallen. He wrote one of the Seven Epistles which are called Catholic.

L.kq3: In illo témpore: Dixit Iesus discípulis suis: Non turbétur cor vestrum. Créditis in Deum, et in me crédite. In domo Patris mei mansiónes multæ sunt. Et réliqua.
L.jqb: Erigénda est nobis, fratres, ad Deum maior inténtio, ut verba sancti Evangélii, quæ modo in nostris áuribus sonuérunt, étiam mente cápere utcúmque possímus. Ait enim Dóminus Iesus: Non turbétur cor vestrum. Créditis in Deum, et in me crédite. Ne mortem tamquam hómines timérent, et ídeo turbaréntur, consolátur eos, étiam se Deum esse contéstans. Créditis, inquit, in Deum, et in me crédite. Cónsequens est enim, ut, si in Deum créditis, et in me crédere debeátis: quod non esset cónsequens, si Christus non esset Deus.

L.g9j: ^℟.^ Quorum doctrína fulget Ecclésia, ut sole luna, allelúia.
L.imv: At that time, Jesus said unto His disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled. Ye believe in God, believe also in Me. In My Father’s house there are many mansions.” And so on.
L.kzw: It behoveth us, my brethren, to have our minds more given toward God, if we would that those words of the Holy Gospel which have just sounded in our ears, should become a living reality for our understandings. The Lord Jesus saith: “Let not your heart be troubled. Ye believe in God, believe also in Me.” Lest, being but men, their heart should be troubled by the fear of death, He strengtheneth them, even by the reminder that He is God. He saith: “Ye believe in God, believe also in Me”, for if ye believe in God, ye must needs believe in Me. And this were not so, if Christ were not God.
L.8o0: * By the light of whose teaching the Church is glorified, even as the moon is glorified by the light of the sun, alleluia.
L.fq0: ^℟.^ By the light of whose teaching the Church is glorified, even as the moon is glorified by the light of the sun, alleluia.
L.j5r: Créditis in Deum, et in eum crédite, cui natúra est, non rapína, esse æquálem Deo; semetípsum enim exinanívit, non tamen formam Dei amíttens, sed formam servi accípiens. Mortem metúitis huic formæ servi: non turbétur cor vestrum; suscitábit illam forma Dei. Sed quid est, quod séquitur: In domo Patris mei mansiónes multæ sunt; nisi quia et sibi metuébant? Unde audíre debuérunt: Non turbétur cor vestrum. Quis enim eórum non metúeret, cum Petro dictum esset, fidentióri atque promptióri: Non cantábit gallus, donec ter me neges?
L.8ql: * Et quasi colúmbæ ad fenéstras suas, allelúia.
L.fwb: ^℟.^ Et quasi colúmbæ ad fenéstras suas, allelúia.
L.oh2: We believe in God, believe also in Him Who is by nature and not by robbery equal with God, for in that He emptied Himself, He did it not by laying aside the form of God, but by taking upon Him the form of a servant. Ye fear death for this form of a servant, but let not your heart be troubled, the form of God will raise it up again. But what signifieth that which followeth: “In My Father’s house there are many mansions.” Was it not that they had fear on their own account, and needed for themselves to hear Him say, “Let not your heart be troubled” Which of them trembled not when they had heard Him say to Peter, the lealest and boldest of them all: “The cock shall not crow this day, before that thou shalt thrice deny that thou knowest Me.”

L.fm8: ^℟.^ And as doves to their windows, alleluia.
L.nrn: Tamquam ergo essent ab illo peritúri, mérito turbabántur; sed cum áudiunt, In domo Patris mei mansiónes multæ sunt; si quo minus, dixíssem vobis: Quia vado paráre vobis locum; a perturbatióne recreántur, certi ac fidéntes, étiam post perícula tentatiónum, se apud Deum cum Christo esse mansúros. Quia etsi álius est álio fórtior, álius álio sapiéntior, álius álio iústior, álius álio sánctior, in domo Patris mei mansiónes multæ sunt. Nullus eórum alienábitur ab illa domo, ubi mansiónem pro suo quisque acceptúrus est mérito.
L.lox: Meetly were they troubled, for that they were about to be scattered from Him, but when they heard Him say, “In My Father’s house are many mansions,” they had been comforted even if He had not also said, “I go to prepare a place for you,” for then they believed and knew, that, when all dangers and all trials were for ever over, they should be for ever with the Lord, with Christ and with God. Yea, though one man be stronger than another, though one be wiser than another, though one be holier than another, yet “in My Father’s house are many mansions.” That house is an house wherein none are strangers, but every man shall receive a mansion therein according as his work shall be.
L.9nh: Deus, qui nos ánnua Apostolórum tuórum Philíppi et Iacóbi solemnitáte lætíficas: præsta, quǽsumus; ut, quorum gaudémus méritis, instruámur exémplis.
L.auh: O God, Who dost every year gladden us by the solemn memorial of thine Apostles Philip and James, grant us grace, we beseech thee, not only to rejoice because of their worthy deeds, but also to tread in their footsteps.

L.m0y: Néreus et Achílleus fratres, eunúchi Fláviæ Domitíllæ, a beáto Petro una cum ipsa eiúsque matre Plautílla baptizáti, cum Domitíllæ persuasíssent, ut virginitátem suam Deo consecráret, ab eius sponso Aureliáno, quod Christiáni essent accusáti, in Póntiam ínsulam relegántur. Mox verbéribus cæsi, ut idólis immolárent, et Tarracínam perdúcti, equúlei et flammárum cruciátibus superátis, secúri percússi sunt; quorum córpora ab Auspício eórum discípulo Romam deláta, via Ardeatína sunt sepúlta. Flávia Domitílla vero, quæ sacrum virginitátis velámen a beáto Cleménte Papa accéperat, et ipsa in ínsulam Póntiam deportáta, et post diutúrna víncula Tarracínam dedúcta, iúdicis iussu incénso eius cubículo, una cum virgínibus Theodóra et Euphrósyna, collactáneis suis, gloriósam mortem oppétiit nonis maii, Traiáno imperatóre; quarum córpora Cæsárius diáconus sepelívit. Pancrátius, nóbili génere in Phrýgia natus, puer quatuórdecim annórum Romæ baptizátus, Diocletiáno et Maximiáno imperatóribus, comprehénditur, et, cum diis sacrificáre constánter renuísset, datis cervícibus, illústrem martýrii corónam consecútus est; cuius corpus ab Octavílla matróna clam via Aurélia sepúltum est.

L.nwv: The brothers Nereus and Achilleus were eunuchs of Flavia Domitilla and were baptized by St. Peter at the same time as she herself and her mother Plautilla. Because they persuaded Domitilla to consecrate her virginity to God, they were accused of being Christians by Aurelian, who had been betrothed to her, and were sent to the island of Ponza. Soon afterwards, they were scourged in an effort to make them sacrifice to idols, and were taken to Terracina, where, after they had overcome the torture of the rack and flaming torches, they were beheaded. Their bodies were taken to Rome by their disciple Auspicius and buried on the Ardeatine Way. As for Flavia Domitilla, who had received the sacred veil of a virgin from Pope St. Clement, she also was deported to the island of Ponza, and after a long imprisonment was taken to Terracina. There, by the judge's orders, her dwelling was set on fire, and she won a glorious death, along with the virgins Theodora and Euphrosyna, her foster-sisters, on May 7, under Emperor Trajan. Their bodies were buried by the Deacon Caesarius. Pancras, born of a noble Phrygian family, was baptized in Rome at the age of fourteen. Under the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, he was arrested; and when he firmly refused to sacrifice to the gods, he was beheaded and so won the glorious crown of martyrdom. His body was buried secretly on the Via Aurelia by the matron Octavilla.

L.8in: ^℣.^ These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes in the Blood of the Lamb.

L.9kh: Dearly beloved brethren, our best way will be to run briefly through the words which have been read from the Holy Gospel, and thereafter rest for a while quietly gazing upon the solemn subject of this great Festival. This is the day whereon “suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” and the Holy Ghost descended upon the Apostles, and, for fleshly minds, gave them minds wherein the love of God was shed abroad and, while without “there appeared unto them cloven tongues, like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them,” within, their hearts were enkindled. While they received the visible presence of God in the form of fire, the flames of His love enwrapped them. The Holy Ghost Himself is love whence it is that John saith “God is love.” Whosoever therefore loveth God with all his soul, already hath obtained Him Whom he loveth, for no man is able to love God, if He have not gained Him Whom he loveth.

L.9e1: But, behold, now, if I shall ask any one of you whether he loveth God, he will answer with all boldness and quietness of spirit: “I do love him.” But at the very beginning of this day's Lesson from the Gospel, ye have heard what the Truth saith: “If a man love Me, he will keep My word.” The test, then, of love, is whether it is showed by works. Hence the same John hath said in his Epistle ^I. iv. 20, v. 3^: “If a man say, I love God, and keepeth not His commandments, He is a liar.” Then do we indeed love God, and keep His commandments, if we deny ourselves the gratification of our appetites. Whosoever still wandereth after unlawful desires, such an one plainly loveth not God, for he saith, Nay, to that which God willeth.

L.aeo: In the words of the Gospel which are this day read, the Lord has spoken unto us in similitudes, touching His flock, and the Door whereby entry is made into their fold. The Pagans therefore may say, “We have good lives,” but if they enter not in the Door, what doth that profit them whereof they make their boast? Good life is profitable to a man if it lead unto life everlasting, but if he does not have life everlasting, what shall his good life profit him? Neither indeed can it be truly said that they live good lives, who are either so blinded as not to know, or so puffed up as to despise, the end of a good life. And no man can have a true and certain hope of life everlasting, unless he know the true Life, Which is Christ, and enter in by that Door into the sheepfold.

These are they who would fain “climb up some other way,” “for to kill and to destroy,” and are not as the Good Shepherd, Who is come to keep and to save. There have been philosophers who have treated many subtle questions of right and wrong, who have been the authors of many distinctions and definitions, who have completed many exceedingly clever arguments, who have filled many books, and have proclaimed their own wisdom with braying trumpets.
